merges.statement: How should spelling count in a comprehension answer, for each kind of task and for typed and spoken answers?

folded_records.statement: How closely a learner's typed quote must match the text is unsettled: one rulebook passes about 95% similarity so tiny slips aren't penalised, another checklist passes only an exact match.
folded_records.detail: The grade-3 rulebook set quote fidelity at 95% similarity, not exact, after a complaint dated 2026-08-17 that the student was penalised for very tiny differences: a Levenshtein ratio of at least 0.95 over normalised strings, with case, quote marks and whitespace folded away. merges.why: The typed-quote record is a special case of the on-record spelling question. merges.statement: Show an on-screen guide or speaking face only at a few key moments, such as the opening and close, not throughout, and never over the teaching visual.

folded_records.statement: Show a speaking face only at a teaching video's open and close, never over the diagram that carries the teaching.

It cites a meta-analysis of 35 studies in which seeing the speaker gave a small retention gain, a null transfer effect, higher social presence and motivation and lower perceived load (Beege et al. 2023). The course's generation spec likewise schedules the speaker's face at the open and at transitions and hides it during dense diagram beats (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g7-science/brainlifts/video-generation-agent-v0.2.md`, line 41).

merges.why: Both records give the same rule. The second record adds that it never sits over the visual that carries the teaching, and the merged sentence keeps that. Neither record is on record. a-guides-words-not-its-looks is left alone because it is about where to spend the effort (the words), not about when the guide appears.

merges.statement: Never let two audio sources play at once, such as music or sound effects under teaching narration, and keep the microphone closed while narration plays.

merges.statement: After a miss or scoring failure, keep the learner's work visible to revise, and let only a fresh correct action pass, never an auto-filled answer or repeated stale selection.

folded_records.statement: Keep the learner's submitted answer in the box after a miss or a scoring failure, so the next try revises it instead of starting over.

merges.statement: In guided practice the lesson supplies part of the answer, never the conclusion, and the learner finishes the reasoning; after one miss rephrase, after two offer a choice.

merges.why: Teaching a complex performance's parts in dependency order, so every rubric row is taught before a full task scores it, is a special case of a lesson assuming only what earlier lessons taught. A full task assumes every row it scores, and exam order is just one order that can break that. Its condition and its AP history evidence narrow the rule but do not change it. merges.statement: Say each thing once and only to teach: no line restating the printed question or anything already said or shown, explaining the obvious, or competing with the learner's action.

merges.statement: Keep a comprehension exchange on one idea for about five turns, each reply building on the learner's answer rather than only judging it, and measure turns per conversation.

folded_records.statement: Shape a comprehension exchange as about five turns built on the learner's answers.

merges.statement: Once learners decode fluently, as expected from grade 3, leave phonics out of vocabulary teaching and break taught words into the parts that carry meaning.

merges.statement: For fluent or upper-grade readers, as in Grade 9 literature, keep read-aloud of the text off by default but available on request, so reading time goes to unaided reading.

merges.statement: Use a synthetic voice only for connective narration and give readings of the text to human voices, since learners can't catch its mispronunciations in verse or older English.

folded_records.statement: Use human readers for verse, older English or any text whose pronunciation learners can't check, since they may learn a synthetic mispronunciation in it as correct.
folded_records.detail: A review of a Grade 9 prototype asked for actors to read the play text aloud, since its language comes through the inflections. The reasoning is a review note, which the document says is offered as rationale and has not been confirmed.

merges.why: Both come from the same review's split of voices: people read the play text, and a synthetic voice reads only the modern connective prose. merges.statement: Write a guide's lines as a welcome, never as a gatekeeper withholding answers, and fix a patronising guide by changing its stance toward the learner, not its words.

folded_records.statement: When a guide character reads as patronising, change its stance toward the learner, such as an elder sharing something precious, rather than simplifying or complicating its words.

A note in the review traces 'patronizing' to stance rather than vocabulary: a young guide explaining things to a child reads as condescension between peers, while an elder sharing something precious reads as initiation (line 190). merges.statement: When adapting a text for young readers, leave unsuitable material out by declared selection, never silent rewriting, and keep hard facts such as coercion or racism visible without endorsing them.

folded_records.detail: Research notes written before a unit on a widely retold epic found its episodes in wide circulation through a new film's trailers and press, a television episode broadcast that year and classroom videos, and noted that a film rated for adults still reaches nine-year-olds through trailers, posters and playground talk (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/research/g4-u1-l2-the-cyclops.md`, lines 510-525). The course's blind-solve validator catches shape tells but cannot catch a question whose answer a child already holds (same note, lines 503-507), so the research set a design rule: no item's correct answer may be a plot fact, every answer is a motive, a clue selection or a category judgement, and every option is quotable from the passage (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/research/g4-u1-l3-circe-and-the-lotus-eaters.md`, lines 500-518). The same research rejected the episode's best-known takeaway as a lesson's target idea, because a child who has never read the passage will produce it, which fails the need-the-text rule at the level of the lesson rather than the item; the decided lesson plan records that reason (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/content/lesson-plans/g4-u1-l2.json`, line 471).

merges.why: Both records make the same point. If readers and models already know a topic or story, the lesson and its items can be answered without the text, so measure that knowledge first and build nothing on it. The retellings record is the well-known-story case of the leak-risk ranking, and it also covers the lesson's target idea. Neither record is on_record, so the more general one is kept.

merges.statement: Fit a test's floor and ceiling, and any items added to an adaptive bank, to where each grade's students sit, not to their average, which can hide either tail.

folded_records.statement: Add items to an adaptive bank at the ability edges where learners actually sit, not around the average.
folded_records.detail: An adaptive reading assessment's design finds the binding constraints on its bank at the ability edges, which differ by grade, a floor in the lower grades and a ceiling in the upper ones, where about 20% of current grade-5 readers sat above even a score of 235 (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/00_BRAINLIFT.md`, line 83). Its bank expansion therefore follows the population rather than the average, with a floor extension and a set of items above the old ceiling. The same line states its pool ratio both ways: 650 items for a 40-item session is 16.3 times the session length, and against a recommended floor of 10 times from the adaptive-testing literature, 400 items, it is 1.6 times the floor, adequate but not lavish. This record's statement also held that an adaptive test needs a bank of at least about ten times its length, which the record size-the-bank-between-two-limits covers.

merges.why: Both records say to set a test's range from where the real students sit, grade by grade, not from their average. The adaptive-bank record applies this to where new bank items go, and both draw on the same assessment package. Its ten-times bank floor is the lower limit already held by size-the-bank-between-two-limits. That record stays separate because sizing a bank between over-exposure and calibration limits is a different rule. Neither merged record is on_record.

merges.statement: When an item, its rubric or a lesson is changed or replaced, give it a new identity, so old answers, verdicts, progress and art don't attach to it.

folded_records.statement: Tie each saved answer and verdict to the version of the item and marking it answered, so a changed item or rubric retires old credit instead of carrying it over.
folded_records.detail: Repairs to a recount's marking, a question's prompt and a dialogue's rubric and reveal each changed the identity of the assessment they touched (`grade3-reading/ui-audit-2026-09-08/BEAD-REGISTER.json`, lines 197, 3373 and 1988). The project ruled that verdicts earned under the old version, a known false pass included, must not restore under the changed assessment. Old records keep their raw bytes and are neither migrated nor deleted: decoders still read them but grant no credit under a new fingerprint.

merges.why: Both state one rule at two sizes. A changed item or rubric must not carry old credit, and a replacement lesson that reuses an identifier must not inherit old progress or art. Both fix this by changing the identity the records are keyed to, and both keep the old records without applying them. Neither was on record before this run. remake-under-new-rules is on record and is about remaking generated content after a rule change, so it is left alone.

merges.statement: A marker can apply a rubric's rule only if it is given what the rule refers to; otherwise enforce the rule in code.

folded_records.statement: When marking a follow-up answer, give the marker the learner's earlier turns, since a follow-up reason can only be judged against what the learner already committed to.
folded_records.detail: The grade-3 rulebook's scoring section has the judge of a comparison turn carry the conversation: its request includes the earlier scored turns, capped at 6 turns of 500 characters each. Without them a follow-up reason such as 'because he sprinkled water' cannot be judged against the trick the child already committed to. The rule was added after a cluster of reports on one comparison question.

merges.why: Special case: a follow-up reason is judged against what the learner already committed to, so the earlier turns are what the marking rule refers to and must reach the marker. The kept record was on record, so its statement stays. The nearby on-record give-the-judge-what-the-student-sees is a different rule and is left alone.

merges.statement: Mark meaning, not wording: any wording that says it counts, a short answer can be enough, and a point made on an earlier try still counts.

folded_records.statement: Mark an answer's stance, not just its keywords: one that hedges or denies the target claim is not strong however many keywords it holds, so ask for a clear claim.
folded_records.detail: An audit of a Grade 5 lesson found that its fallback marker graded free answers by overlap with target facts, with coverage of 0.5 or 4 raw hits counting as strong, so a hedged, negated or off-topic answer that contained the right keywords scored as correct. The course's bar says the evaluator must read stance, not tokens, and the fix checks for negation and hedge markers before the coverage threshold and sends such answers back with a prompt to commit to a clear claim. It was re-verified on hedged and negated answers at full coverage, which both now come back as needing work.

merges.why: Same rule from the strict side. Reading stance rather than keywords is marking meaning rather than wording. A hedged or negated answer that holds the keywords does not say the point, so under 'any wording that says it counts' it does not count. The kept record was on record, so its statement stays.

merges.statement: Let no access need block participation, use equivalent access modes only where what is measured stays unchanged, so reading-test passages are never read aloud, and disclose supports that change it.

folded_records.statement: In a reading test, read-aloud support may voice the questions and answer options but never the passage, because a passage heard rather than read measures listening comprehension.
folded_records.detail: A reading assessment's accommodations rule allows text-to-speech on question stems and answer choices but never on passages, because passages read aloud measure listening comprehension, not reading; it mirrors the reference test, whose per-part control and guidance exclude reading passages (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/skill/SKILL.md`, `grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/red-team/RED_TEAM_RESPONSE.md`). Its passage requirements also call for cold, silent reading with no audio (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/reference/CAT_MAP_EXAM_SPEC.md`). An audit found its accommodations note had claimed text-to-speech before the product had any, and the feature then shipped for stems and choices only (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/red-team/ADDRESS_STATUS.md`). The rule is for scored reading tests; in teaching, a text may be read aloud in full.

merges.why: The read-aloud rule is a special case of the general one. An access mode counts as equivalent only if what is measured stays the same. A reading-test passage that is heard measures listening, not reading, while voicing the questions and options leaves the measure as it was. Both records are new in this run, so the general one is kept with a statement that includes the reading-test case. The on-record text fallback for spoken answers is close but narrower and adds its own scoring point (recognition errors, accent and noise), and keeping it would leave its statement unchanged and lose the general rule, so it stays separate. The other records in this section say different things and are left alone.

merges.statement: Judge whether one measure, such as a model marker, can replace another by how far and which way individual scores differ, not by correlation, which misses a uniformly generous marker.

folded_records.statement: Validate a model marker on its signed gap from human marks and its rate of false highs, not on correlation alone, which a uniformly generous marker can still pass.
folded_records.detail: A grade 4-5 writing module's calibration spec reports, for each skill and band, exact and adjacent agreement, a weighted kappa and the mean of model minus human marks, because a correlation cannot show a uniform offset. It reports false highs, a weak answer given full marks, apart from false lows as the safety-critical error, and predicts from difficulty-estimation research that a model marker will be systematically too generous, more so with a bigger model. The seed baseline it reuses reported 87.5% agreement (42/48) with 1 false high.

merges.why: Both records are new. A model marker standing in for human marks is one case of one measure standing in for another. Both say correlation hides how far and which way individual scores differ, so judge on that gap.

merges.statement: Judge any gain against the growth that students with the same starting score, grade and weeks of instruction make anyway, which is small for stronger students in later grades.

folded_records.statement: Judge a student's growth against students who started at the same score in the same grade with the same weeks of instruction, because expected growth differs with each.
folded_records.detail: A reading assessment package takes the reference test's conditional growth percentile as its key diagnostic output: how much a student grew relative to peers with the same prior score, the same grade and the same weeks of instruction, which controls for starting ability and asks whether the student grew more or less than expected (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/MAP_PROXY_VALIDITY_CASE.md`). The publisher's 2025 norms in the same document put typical fall-to-spring growth at about 11 points in grade 2, 9 in grade 3, 6 in grade 4 and 5 in grade 5, so the same gain means more in grade 5 than in grade 2. The grade 2 figure rounds a difference of 11.6 points, from 170.1 to 181.7.

merges.why: Both records are new and state one rule: a gain means something only against the growth expected anyway at the same grade and starting level. One adds weeks of instruction and the other adds projected gains.

merges.statement: When students took different items or forms, never compare or correlate their raw or percent-correct scores; first equate them, or estimate ability from the answers and each item's difficulty.

folded_records.statement: Correlate scores from two tests only on equated scales, because percent-correct on forms of differing difficulty is not one scale, so the result is an artifact, not a finding.
folded_records.detail: A Grade 7 reading plan tried to link its students' results to an external state test and found 60 students tested on both, which established only that the link exists. The stored state-test score was percent-correct on released forms of differing difficulty across years, range 0.8–97.5, not an equated scale score, while the other measure was a scale score averaged across seasons. A correlation on the 60 returned r≈−0.16 (ρ≈−0.06), which the plan recorded as a verified negative: a confounded artifact, not a finding. It claims neither a direction nor a size until equated scale scores, or a per-form raw-to-scale conversion, are available.

merges.why: Both records are new and rest on one rule: scores from item sets of differing difficulty are not on one scale. Correlating pooled percent-correct with another test is one case of comparing such scores across students.

merges.statement: Keep machine checks apart from human judgment: a quality call stays unjudged until a person has watched or listened, and an AI judge only picks what that person reviews.

folded_records.statement: A page-wide overflow or geometry check is not a visual pass, so inspect rendered screens by eye: off-screen pop-ups, cropped faces and squeezed labels all pass it.
folded_records.detail: In a staging sweep every recorded page-level width check was clear while a fixed glossary pop-up sat mostly off-screen and portrait art lost a character's head, and the report notes that page-level horizontal-overflow checks do not catch that pop-up. A later laptop sweep of 475 screenshots found no document-level horizontal overflow, yet looking at them confirmed two new defects, teaching explanations struck through and an undo label squeezed into stacked words. The project's regression notes say not to replace visual inspection with an overflow count, and that a merge or passing geometry check is not a visual retest.

merges.why: The new record is a special case of the on-record one. A page-wide overflow or geometry check is a machine check, and a visual pass is a quality call a person makes by eye. The kept statement already covers it, so it stays as it is.

merges.statement: Check every line a model writes at answer time against house rules and the authored text beside it, repairing rather than discarding what fails, such as praise repeating the answer.

folded_records.statement: Where generated praise sits beside an authored answer, measure their overlap in code and trim the praise: the two writers can't see each other, and an instruction is a request.
folded_records.detail: In a reading course, the praise for a passed open answer is composed by the scoring model at answer time, while the full answer printed with it was authored with the lesson; both reached for the same sentence, so the child read their own answer twice in one breath (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/rules/questions-and-assessment.md`, lines 442-450). Telling the scorer that the full answer follows and to name only what the child did made this rare, and the overlap is now also measured at runtime: `grade3-reading/course-renderer/src/lib/scoring/echo.ts` scores the share of the praise's content words that the answer already contains and cuts the praise back to its acknowledgement above a threshold, pinned by `grade3-reading/course-renderer/scripts/echo.test.mjs` against the real reply that prompted the rule (lines 452-460 and 494-497 of the rule file). The rule file puts the repetition worth catching at the seam between a written line and a generated one, the only place nobody is reading.

merges.why: The praise record is a special case of the answer-time record. Generated praise is a line a model writes at answer time, and the authored answer is the authored text beside it. Measuring their overlap is the check, and trimming is the repair rather than a discard. Neither record is on_record, so I kept the broader one. I left quote-the-learner-word-for-word and point-to-a-place-only-when-known alone because each adds a reference of its own: the learner's exact words, or the excerpt positions the model was given. I also left close pairs where an on_record statement does not cover the new rule: a transcript of learner speech versus a generated clip, a keyed quote in a passage versus a mark in a quotation, a debt list that only shrinks versus exemptions that can be granted, and a copy guard's run test versus guards in general.

merges.statement: If automated marking fails, spend no try and give no verdict; after repeated failures, show the authored answer, let the learner move on, and label it unchecked, not earned.

folded_records.statement: When scoring fails, spend no try and give no verdict; after repeated failures, show the authored answer, let the learner move on, and say it wasn't checked.
folded_records.detail: In a Grade 3 reading course, a scorer outage showed learners a notice saying 'Nothing is wrong with what you said', a claim of correctness no judgment supported, since an unscored turn has no verdict. The course's retry design counts such a turn as unscored, so no scored try is spent and no completion is banked, and the fix reuses its existing neutral line saying the answer has not been checked and can be sent again. Its published rules add that a gate which lets a learner past after repeated failures shows the authored answer first, and the retry design keeps the learner's draft until they choose to move on.

merges.why: Both records give the same rule in different words. When scoring fails, the learner loses no try and gets no verdict. After repeated failures they see the authored answer, move on, and the result is labelled unchecked. Neither record was on record before this run. The kept one sits in the AI-marker group and has the fuller statement, adding that the result is never counted as earned. Other close records in this slice say different things. Two examples: the cold-text gate adds transfer to an unseen text, which the on-record rule about advancing on mastery does not cover, and the rule on evidence spanning two sentences is different from the on-record rule about whole selectable pieces. Those are left alone, and so are all pairs where both records are on record.

merges.statement: A marking guide describes the reasoning that earns credit in a few checks, not facts or keywords, which can be wrong or matched by an answer lacking the reasoning.

folded_records.statement: Mark an argument on whether the claim answers the question, the evidence is relevant and sufficient, the reasoning links them and the counterclaim is answered, not just on matched quotes.
folded_records.detail: The Grade 9 strategy names as one of its two largest risks a judge that grades evidence by keyword when the grade asks for reasoning, and answers it with rubric criteria for relevant and sufficient evidence and for reasoning that links them, after the grade 9-10 standard on delineating and evaluating an argument. Its research brief puts the shift as one from finding the clue to choosing the best evidence and explaining it, so the model's rubric should grade how relevant and sufficient the evidence is, and the reasoning, not just whether a matching span was found. An earlier design canvas shows the learner where their argument stands, check by check, from the claim answering the question to the counterclaim being answered. In the built prototype the judge is still rules, not a model, so the rubric has not been tried.

merges.why: The argument record applies the general rule to arguments. Its claim, evidence, reasoning and counterclaim checks are the few reasoning checks, and its matched quotes are the keywords an answer can hit without the reasoning. Its source risk is grading evidence by keyword when the task asks for reasoning, which is the second failure the kept record names. The kept record already cites scoring the claim-evidence relationship rather than a phrase, quotes failing closed, and a check for the counter-case. It is on_record, so its statement stays as it is. The other new record, require-the-criterion-the-task-is-for, says something different: the target content must be required so that other criteria cannot outvote it. Neither keyword matching nor rubric levels covers that, so it stays separate.

merges.statement: Give every open-ended task or exchange a defined end, such as a completed paragraph or a sign the idea is understood, so it doesn't run until someone gives up.

folded_records.statement: Give every open-ended task a defined end point, such as a completed paragraph, because an exchange without one ends only when someone gives up.
folded_records.detail: In a Grade 9 prototype's quote break-down chat, the learner's second answer was substantively wrong, the guide half-corrected it and moved on, and nothing told the learner or the app when the quote had been understood. Its review contrasted a stem-based task, which ends when the paragraph is complete, with a chat, which ends when someone gives up, and made a convergence criterion a checklist item.

merges.why: Both come from the same prototype review of a quote break-down chat and state one rule: an open-ended task or exchange needs a defined end point, or it runs until someone gives up. Both are new; the one whose detail cites its source is kept.

merges.statement: Make an on-screen guide an encouraging mentor more expert than the learner, not a peer, shown only at a few key moments and, for teenagers, never cartoonish or over-praising.

folded_records.statement: Make an on-screen guide a mentor more competent than the learner, not a peer, joining expertise with encouragement, since studies found that role gave the best learning.
folded_records.detail: The Grade 9 video-design notes summarise a study that built three agent roles, an authoritative expert, an encouraging motivator and a mentor blending both, and tested them in two experiments (N=78, N=71), in which the mentor produced the best combined learning-and-motivation outcome (`g9/library/collections/g3-repo-initiative-g9-othello-2026-10-01/research/video-02-instructional-video-design.md`, lines 45-50). The notes on AI classmates describe the same study by its gains, the expert raising information acquisition, the motivator self-efficacy and the mentor both learning and motivation, in college students (`g9/library/collections/g3-repo-initiative-g9-othello-2026-10-01/research/idea-02-ai-classmates-multi-agent-debate.md`, lines 15-18). The Grade 9 lesson design specification cites the result for its guide, a mentor who makes students think hard and aids the journey to the answer rather than giving it (`g9/library/text/L9b6d99.txt`, lines 20 and 278).

folded_records.statement: Show an on-screen guide or speaking face only at a few key moments, such as the opening and close, not throughout, and never over the teaching visual.
folded_records.detail: The review of a Grade 9 prototype asked to reduce the guide's continuous face time and keep strategic appearances at the opening, the key idea and the handover (`g9/library/text/L36b8ba.txt`, line 71); its evidence notes say a visible speaker reliably improves motivation rather than learning and can add cognitive load, naming no study (line 414). A comparison of three opening films on one rubric found that in one of them 23 of the 25 shots without the guide carried their line, against 2 of 11 with the guide on camera (`g9/library/text/L88a690.txt`, line 35). The shot verdicts are judgements against each line, not viewing data.

merges.why: Judged as two separate pairs. Each record is one part of this one: the mentor-role record states its first rule (a mentor joining expertise with encouragement, from the same agent-role study), and the key-beats record states its second (the guide appears only at a few set moments, not throughout). This record already states both rules, so both fold into it. All three are new.

merges.statement: Fix in advance the order in which a time-boxed lesson's parts give way for a slow learner: enrichment and untested items first, never what a later part depends on.

folded_records.statement: In a time-boxed lesson, decide in advance the order in which optional parts give way when a learner is slow, and list the parts that are never dropped.
folded_records.detail: A Grade 3 lesson design checks every time against an accepted 22 to 29 minute window and writes an ordered drop ladder of ten rungs for a slow child, each row giving what it saves and why it can go, starting with enrichment already conditional on spare time (`g9/library/text/L8d5159.txt`, lines 2 and 351-396). Below it sits a list never dropped whatever the clock says: the read-aloud, since without the text there is no lesson; the taught word, which the unaided task cashes and breaks without; the comprehension checks; the modelled write-up step; and the unaided task, the only unaided evidence the lesson produces (lines 397-418). The design restates the list for a struggling learner as what is never traded (line 111).

merges.why: Both state the same rule from the same Grade 3 lesson design's drop ladder for a slow learner: fix in advance the order in which parts give way, starting with enrichment, next to a list of parts that never drop. Both are new.

merges.statement: When a routine has the learner reread a stretch of text, narrow the view to it and pause narration until they say they have, so they do the reading.

folded_records.statement: When modelling how to find the right part of a text, narrow the view to that stretch, ask the learner to reread it, and pause narration until they have.
folded_records.detail: The reading curriculum's Locate routine, woven into its modelling moments, zooms the view to the pertinent stretch of about 60-120 words, tells the child to reread it, and pauses narration until the child has (`othello-course-renderer-draft/repo/docs/pedagogy/modelling-moment-procedures.md`, line 844). The course renderer adopted it as a rule, because without the stop the reread is only a line the guide says while the child watches, when the routine exists so that the child does the finding (`othello-course-renderer-draft/repo/docs/rules/pedagogy-and-lesson-structure.md`, lines 359-368). Its think-aloud node pauses narration at the handover mark and resumes only on the child's tap (lines 373-375).

merges.why: Both describe the same locate routine from the same reading course, with the same stretch of about 60 to 120 words: narrow the view, hand the reread to the learner and hold the narration until they have done it. Both are new.

merges.statement: Define a historical term for a group of people briefly at its first use, and say it plainly and respectfully, with no caricature, stereotype or exoticised accent.

folded_records.statement: Say historical terms for people plainly and respectfully, explain each at its first use, and give no person or term an exoticized accent.
folded_records.detail: A Grade 9 film's recording manifest bars an exoticized accent for any character or historical term, and its delivery notes ask for a historical term for a person to be spoken plainly and respectfully, as the sound plan repeats. The film script explains that term the first time it is spoken.

merges.why: Both give the same rule for the same unit's historical term, from its script and recording notes: explain it briefly at first use and say it plainly and respectfully, with no stereotype or exoticised accent. The statement keeps to historical terms because the voice record says its evidence covers only one term. Both are new.

merges.statement: After a wrong answer, keep the attempt visible, diagnose its misconception, and pass only the learner's own fresh correction, never an auto-filled answer or a repeated stale selection.

folded_records.statement: After a miss or scoring failure, keep the learner's work visible to revise, and let only a fresh correct action pass, never an auto-filled answer or repeated stale selection.
folded_records.detail: A Grade 5 lesson's acceptance checklist restates a release-gate rule: a wrong attempt stays displayed, preserved and diagnosed, and passing needs a fresh correct action made by the learner, so the interface never fills in the answer or lets the same stale selection pass. Its check answers wrong twice with different wrong answers, confirms both stay visible and blocked with support after the second, and confirms that only a new explicit correct selection shows Next.

merges.why: Both state the same rule from overlapping reading-course rule sets: a wrong attempt stays visible and is diagnosed, and only the learner's own fresh correction passes, never an auto-filled answer. Both are new.

merges.statement: Make each evidence tap or highlight a decision that can be wrong and is then discussed, steered to the parts that matter, since untrained highlighting is rated low utility.

folded_records.statement: Don't count marking evidence as learning in itself: make each tap or highlight a decision that can be wrong and is then argued about.
folded_records.detail: Lesson research for an evidence lesson cites a review of learning techniques that rates highlighting and underlining as low utility, against practice testing and distributed practice as high utility, because most students over-highlight and highlighters were at a disadvantage on inference questions. It draws one conclusion for a tap-the-evidence interaction: the tap is not itself the learning, and what makes it work is that the tap is a decision that can be wrong and is then argued about.

merges.why: Both state the same rule from the same review of learning techniques: a tap or highlight is not learning in itself and works only as a decision that can be wrong and is then discussed. Both are new.

merges.statement: Whether a self-paced lesson with no adult present should handle violence more cautiously than adult-led editions, with one warning line, brief reporting and no picture, awaits a ruling.

folded_records.statement: In lessons a child takes alone, treat frightening content more cautiously than classroom texts that rely on an adult: one warning line, brief reporting and no picture of violence.
folded_records.detail: Research for a lesson on a violent episode found that mainstream material for younger children prints far more than expected, with a class magazine printing four lines of detail for eight and nine year olds, but those precedents rely on an adult: a class magazine read with an adult present, and a curriculum with a briefed adult and a letter home (`othello-course-renderer-draft/repo/content/lesson-plans/g4-u1-l2.json`, lines 516-518). The brief recommended one guide line before the passage and restraint in the printed text, with violence reported in one clause or as one action and its result and no image of it, since a picture is not read aloud, cannot be paced and cannot be argued about in an app with no adult present (`othello-course-renderer-draft/repo/docs/research/g4-u1-l2-the-cyclops.md`, lines 795-817). The lesson plan records this as a proposal, with the one sentence that goes below published practice awaiting sign-off (the plan, lines 516-518).

merges.why: Both come from the same grade 4 lesson research and state the same proposal: one warning line, brief reporting and no picture of violence when no adult is present. Its lesson plan records the proposal as still awaiting sign-off, so the open-question record is kept and the rule version folds into it. Both are new.

merges.statement: Put no length floor or ceiling on a learner's answer: a short right answer is secure, and independent practice, writing included, is never capped in time or space.

folded_records.statement: Never cap independent practice, including writing, at a fixed length of time or space, so it can expand as learners gain expertise.
folded_records.detail: A Grade 9 lesson design specification says independent practice grows as students gain expertise and must never be capped at a fixed length, repeats in its timing rules that it is never capped, and asks the build for an uncapped writing space (`g9/sources/Year 9 ELA_ Lesson Design Specification for Devfactory.md`, lines 174, 245 and 292). Its lesson profiles move independent practice from 20% of a first-encounter lesson to 65% of an expert one (lines 216-222).

merges.why: Both cite the same Grade 9 lesson design specification: independent practice, writing included, is never capped at a fixed length. That rule is the no-ceiling half of this record, so the other record folds in and the statement keeps both halves. Both are new.

merges.statement: Pre-teach only words without which comprehension breaks down; support the rest in place, replace them or teach them after reading, and never introduce a word by asking what it means.

folded_records.statement: Before reading, teach only the words whose absence would break understanding, and teach the rest afterwards.
folded_records.detail: A Grade 3 reading red-team standard takes two vocabulary criteria from chapter 3 of the vocabulary-instruction book Bringing Words to Life: only the words needed to prevent a breakdown in comprehension are taught before reading and the rest after it, and an unfamiliar word is never introduced with a guess-opener such as 'who can tell me what X means?'. The same standard separates light glossing during reading from the few words taught to production after the read. Both criteria are adopted rules checked by a model judge, and nothing here measured them.

merges.why: Same rule in other words. Both records quote the same line from two documents: only the words needed to prevent comprehension breakdown are pre-taught, and the rest are taught after reading. I kept the record that is already contested and has the example, since both records carry counter-evidence. The folded record's ban on opening a new word with a guess goes into the statement so it is not lost.

merges.statement: Introduce related new words as the structure they form, such as a web showing the concept and how the rest relate to it, not as a deck of equal cards.

folded_records.statement: Introduce related new words as the structure they form, showing which word is the concept and how the others relate to it, rather than as a row of equal cards.
folded_records.detail: A review of a Grade 9 prototype dropped a deck of tap-to-reveal word cards as a priority item, since the word web already introduced the words and could show how they relate. Its note argues that the words are not a list but a structure, one naming the concept, some describing the person and others naming the mechanism, which a row of equal cards hides.

merges.why: Same learning from the same review note about the same six-word card deck, cited from two copies of that note: the words form a structure, a web shows it and equal cards hide it. I kept the record whose detail says the note is unconfirmed rationale. The statement adds the folded record's point that the structure shows which word is the concept.

merges.statement: Don't build help or independent work on a text as a chat thread: independent practice should produce the learner's own writing in a structured frame, not conversation turns.

folded_records.statement: Don't run a learner's work on a text as a chat with a guide: independent practice should produce the learner's own writing in a structured frame, not conversation turns.
folded_records.detail: A review of a Grade 9 lesson prototype found independent practice built as a chat thread, at the point where the learner should be producing writing alone, which it called the furthest thing from the deliverable. Having raised the point four times across two units, it set a standing requirement that the guide is not a chatbot, since typing an answer into a conversation and getting a reply is the wrong model of studying a text and the wrong message about where answers come from. It asked for the chat thread to be replaced with the same stem grid as guided practice. A build meeting the next day recorded that the chat-based approach had been discarded.

merges.why: Both come from the same review of a Grade 9 prototype and quote the same standing requirement against the chat pattern, along with the same note from the next day that the chat approach was discarded. One rules out chat for help and for independent writing. The other adds what to do instead: the learner's own writing in a structured frame. Neither record was on record before this run. I kept the broader one because it also covers help. All other records in this section say different things and are left alone, including close pairs such as the two sentence-frame rules and the two rules about formats kept out of scoring.

merges.statement: Keep help quiet and optional: glosses, notes and a few named helpers open only when the learner asks or with feedback, never as a constant guide or per-part buttons.

folded_records.statement: During reading, keep glosses and background notes pulled: a quiet mark opens one only when the learner asks, and no help button sits beside every part.
folded_records.detail: An early lesson script for a 3D version of the Grade 9 lessons put a help button beside each part of the reading, and per-part help was later removed as having overloaded the learning (`othello-archive/sources/l1-script/Othello Lesson 1 (1.1)_ Lesson Script v3, Stage 1.txt`, line 102; `othello-archive/src/steps/Reading.tsx`, line 3). What stayed is pulled, never pushed: a glossed word carries a dotted underline whose gloss opens in the side panel when tapped, never on hover alone, and background notes added after review feedback sit as quiet marks beside their lines, open only if the learner asks, and must never answer a checkpoint (`othello-archive/DESIGN.md`, line 23; `othello-archive/src/content/context.ts`, lines 1-4).

merges.why: Both state one rule: help stays quiet and the learner pulls it; nothing pushes it. The reading record is the special case for glosses and background notes. Its 'no help button beside every part' is the 'never a constant guide' clause applied to a text. Neither record was on record. Two close records stay separate: offer-help-never-pick-the-answer forbids picking the answer automatically after misses, and stage-supports-dont-stack-them brings each support in at its own step to limit live targets.

merges.statement: Help may paraphrase a hard line, say who speaks to whom or ask planned questions that draw out reasoning, but the interpretation, evidence and answer stay the learner's.

folded_records.statement: In independent practice a guide may ask planned questions that draw out the student's reasoning, but never supplies the interpretation, chooses the evidence or revises the answer.
folded_records.detail: In one unit's oral lesson the guide asks questions during independent practice, and the unit's design brief bars agents from choosing evidence, suggesting interpretations or revising the response. Review drew the line between questions that elicit the student's reasoning and hints that supply it: the guide may ask the planned questions and listen, while the student supplies the interpretation, evidence and explanation.

merges.why: Both draw the same line for help: it may clarify or ask questions that bring out the learner's own thinking, but it never does the interpretive work. One names line paraphrase and the other names planned questions. The line-help record already allowed one directing question, and the questions record adds evidence and revision to what stays with the learner. Neither record was on record. leave-the-hunt-to-the-learner stays separate: it was on record and is about not narrowing an open search.

merges.statement: Nothing a student sees or hears may give the answer before the first attempt, including the picture behind a paused question.

folded_records.statement: In guided practice, nothing the frame supplies may carry the answer: no filled slot holds the gap's word or a synonym, and on an inference the guide states no claim.
folded_records.detail: In one reading course's guided step, the child finishes a started sentence whose evidence slot is already filled and one gap is left, and a rule of 3 July pitches the filled slot at situation or behaviour level, never the gap's word or a synonym of it (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/pedagogy/lesson-architecture.md`, lines 65-68). The procedure spec flags the variation on feelings as a structural risk, because its modelled step already names the feeling, so the frame must never reprint that conclusion. A later contract change made the guide's opening claim optional after a review found that the claim on an inference page gave the answer away: a page that teaches finding keeps the claim to frame the hunt for proof, while an inference page authors none and opens on the frame's prompt (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/process/CONTRACT-SIGNOFFS.md`, lines 140-147).

folded_records.statement: Nothing pre-filled in a frame or said just before its blank may contain the gap's answer word or a synonym; pitch the filled part at situation or behaviour level.
folded_records.detail: The answer-distance rule in a reading curriculum's modelling procedures, which notes for a Grade 5 audit file as the leak discriminator, says pre-filled text in evidence slots must never contain the gap's word or a synonym, so the child types only the thinking gap. A later walk of four built lessons found guided and independent steps giving their answers away before the child tried, among them a guided step whose guide line stated the decision right before the blank that asked for it; the fix had the line say only that a decision is made.

folded_records.statement: Show an ordering item's parts out of their correct order, and check it in code, so a learner who moves nothing cannot pass.
folded_records.detail: A reading course's review procedure turns every fixed defect class into a validator rule the same day, proved first to fire on the old defect, and lists sequence items in their presented order among its precedents (`grade3-reading/.claude/skills/reviewer-round/SKILL.md`, lines 81-84). The validator fails any sequence item whose presented order equals its key, because a child who presses Check without moving a card would pass an ordering task by doing no ordering, and it records that both of that grade's sequence items had shipped in the correct order and were caught by it (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/scripts/validate-contracts.mjs`, lines 815-827). Every build specification now carries the rule (`grade3-reading/.claude/skills/lesson-build/SKILL.md`, line 27).

merges.why: These are special cases of the older record, which keeps its statement. Four things each show or tell the student the answer before the first attempt: a frame whose filled part holds the gap's word or a synonym, a line just before the blank that states the decision, a claim printed on an inference page, and an ordering item shown in its correct order. The two frame records are also one rule in other words and cite the same answer-distance rule. The older record's evidence already holds answers handed over by nudges and instructions, and position leaks in sequence items. None of the three was on record. Left apart: make-the-target-thinking-unavoidable also covers the ordering case, a pass with nothing moved, but it is on record, so it is not merged with this one. evidence-that-doesnt-give-itself-away stays separate because it adds its own construction rules for two-part items: an arbitrary passage detail and a keyed quote that doesn't announce itself.

merges.statement: Hold the question until a learner reading alone could plausibly have read the text, timed from its word count at a generous reading rate for their age.

folded_records.statement: In self-paced reading, hold the next step until the learner could plausibly have read the chunk at a pace suited to their age, so they can't skip to the question.
folded_records.detail: A Grade 5 lesson's acceptance checklist requires, in read-it-myself mode, that each chunk's advance control stays disabled until a minimum time, derived from the chunk's word count at an age-plausible reading rate, has passed, and checks it by clicking Next at once and timing the unlock. A Grade 3 course's lesson rules set the same kind of hold: the door to each chunk's recall-only stop arms when the read-aloud ends or, when the child reads alone, after the longer of 4 seconds and the chunk's words at 150 words a minute.

merges.why: This is one rule in other words. Both hold back the question after a passage until a learner reading alone could plausibly have read it, timed from its word count, so it can't be reached by clicking straight through. Both cite the same hold: the longer of 4 seconds and the time to read the words at 150 a minute. One adds the blocking wait and a generous rate ceiling, the other a pace suited to the learner's age, and the statement holds both. The kept record has the fuller evidence and counter-evidence. Neither was on record. Left apart: make-the-target-thinking-unavoidable is on record and says something different, since a time floor does not make the reading itself unavoidable.
